Compute Impulse Response Function (IRF)

Source: R/irf.R
IRF.Rd

This function calculates the impulse response function (IRF) of a time series model. The IRF describes how a model's variables react to external shocks over time.

IRF(x, ...)

Arguments

x

A fitted model object, such as from a VAR or ARIMA model. This model is used to compute the impulse response.

...

Additional arguments to be passed to lower-level functions.

Details

If new_data contains the .impulse column, those values will be treated as impulses for the calculated impulse responses.

The impulse response function provides insight into the dynamic behaviour of a system in response to external shocks. It traces the effect of a one-unit change in the impulse variable on the response variable over a specified number of periods.

For a mable, the number of periods is specified using h (or by providing new_data). Model specific options are passed via ..., for example fable::VAR() models accept impulse (the name of the variable to shock) and orthogonal (whether to compute orthogonalised impulse responses).

Examples

library(fable)
library(tsibble)
#> 
#> Attaching package: ‘tsibble’
#> The following objects are masked from ‘package:base’:
#> 
#>     intersect, setdiff, union

# Annual GDP growth and CPI inflation (%) for Australia
aus_economy <- tsibbledata::global_economy %>%
  dplyr::filter(Country == "Australia") %>%
  dplyr::transmute(Growth, Inflation = 100 * difference(log(CPI))) %>%
  dplyr::filter(!is.na(Growth), !is.na(Inflation))

fit <- aus_economy %>%
  model(VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1)))

# Response of both variables to a unit shock in GDP growth
fit %>%
  IRF(h = 10, impulse = "Growth")
#> # A tsibble: 10 x 4 [1Y]
#> # Key:       .model [1]
#>    .model                                Year   Growth Inflation
#>    <chr>                                <dbl>    <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2018  1           0    
#>  2 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2019  0.219       0.373
#>  3 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2020 -0.00638     0.415
#>  4 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2021 -0.0617      0.368
#>  5 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2022 -0.0670      0.305
#>  6 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2023 -0.0591      0.248
#>  7 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2024 -0.0490      0.199
#>  8 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2025 -0.0397      0.159
#>  9 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2026 -0.0319      0.127
#> 10 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2027 -0.0255      0.102

# Orthogonalised response to a shock in inflation
fit %>%
  IRF(h = 10, impulse = "Inflation", orthogonal = TRUE)
#> # A tsibble: 10 x 4 [1Y]
#> # Key:       .model [1]
#>    .model                                Year  Growth Inflation
#>    <chr>                                <dbl>   <dbl>     <dbl>
#>  1 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2018  0          1.70 
#>  2 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2019 -0.248      1.52 
#>  3 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2020 -0.275      1.26 
#>  4 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2021 -0.244      1.03 
#>  5 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2022 -0.203      0.825
#>  6 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2023 -0.164      0.660
#>  7 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2024 -0.132      0.528
#>  8 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2025 -0.106      0.422
#>  9 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2026 -0.0846     0.337
#> 10 VAR(vars(Growth, Inflation) ~ AR(1))  2027 -0.0676     0.270
